cases.quote: EN: The width of math symbols (cl-17) and math operators (cl-18) is full-width, i.e. one em (see Figure 176). — JA: 等号類（cl-17）及び演算記号（cl-18）の字幅は，全角とする（Figure 176）．
cases.rationale: §A.17 keys 45 members by the UCS column and U+003D EQUALS SIGN is its first row. Every one of the 45 Remarks (備考) cells is empty in both renderings, so Appendix A qualifies no member of this class by frame (字幅), by writing direction or by role, and §A.17 carries no prose at all: the heading is followed immediately by the table and the table is followed by the next heading. Every qualification cl-17 has lives in §3.7.4 and §3.9.2 and is reached only by cross-reference. All 45 keys are listed a second time under §A.27, where the Remarks cell reads 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」, so no code point belongs to cl-17 alone and every cl-17 occurrence carries at least two candidate listings before the caller says anything. The frame is what separates them, and the sentence that fills §A.17's silence about it is the quoted one from §3.7.4 — the only statement of cl-17's 字幅 anywhere in the document. This occurrence declares the one em that sentence names, so §A.27's qualification does not describe it and cl-17 is what is left standing. §3.7.4 is deliberately not cited in `rules`: what a classification answer exercises is §3.9.2's grouping and the first of §3.9.1's axes, while §3.7.4's own rules — the width, the four spacings and the break permission — are composition rules whose cases a later milestone writes.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.17, first row, against §A.27's Remarks column (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.27 lists 003D with the Remarks cell 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」, which an occurrence declared one em wide does not satisfy. §3.9.1 asks 'Is the character width full-width, half-width, or something else?' / 「文字・記号の字幅は，全角か，半角か，又はそれ以外か．」 first among the ways positioning differs, so the answer may not be reached without reading the declared frame. Answering cl-27 for every U+003D is answering from the code point rather than from the occurrence (ADR 0008).

Keying on the English class name. cl-17 is named 'Math symbols' in English and 等号類 — the equals-sign group — in Japanese, and it holds the relations; cl-18 is 'Math operators' / 演算記号 and holds ＋－÷×. The English names read backwards from ordinary mathematical usage, where an equals sign is not what a mathematician calls a symbol and a plus is not what one calls an operator, and §3.9.2's own first Note under the cl-17 item states them backwards as well. An implementation must key on the class number and on §A.17's table; §A.17 lists 003D and §A.18's six rows do not.

cases.quote: EN: Is the character width full-width, half-width, or something else? — JA: 文字・記号の字幅は，全角か，半角か，又はそれ以外か．
cases.rationale: The same code point as the case above on a different frame (字幅), and the answer is a different class — which is the whole reason a class is a function of an occurrence and not of a code point. §A.27 lists 003D with the Remarks cell 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」 and this occurrence declares exactly that frame, so §A.27's sentence describes it. §A.17's own row states nothing about width, but the class it enumerates does have one: §3.7.4 states that the 字幅 of math symbols (等号類) is one em, and a proportionally set equals sign is not that, so the two listings do not both survive here either. The advance is the caller's measurement of a proportional glyph and is not what decides this: the frame is declared, never inferred from the advance (ADR 0002), and a proportional glyph exactly one em wide would be undecidable if it were.

forbidden.why: Answering cl-17 for every U+003D discards the only thing §A.27's Remarks column says about this key, and gives one answer for this case and for A.17/equals-sign/frame-full-em, which are the same key on two frames. §3.7.4 states that the width of math symbols (cl-17) is one em, so an equals sign the caller measured proportionally is not being set as one.

cases.quote: However, there are some ambiguous cases, such as "エディター（editor）は……". In this case, English spelling is indicated using parentheses in a Japanese line of text. In this particular case, Japanese design is better.
cases.rationale: U+003D is named by two Appendix A tables, §A.17 and §A.27, and the only thing separating them is §A.27's Remarks qualification, which is a statement about the frame (字幅). A caller who declares no frame has supplied nothing that separates them, and §3.9.2 does not decide the case: it concedes an ambiguity over one example and says one design is 'better', which is a preference, is stated about that one example, and names no class. Both survivors are therefore recorded here rather than one, each with the policy question that selects it. This project answers with the lowest-numbered survivor, published in docs/decisions/ambiguous-context.md, and that is what the empty overlay selects. Nothing in the input hints at the answer: the advance is one em and the frame is still unstated, because ADR 0002 forbids inferring one from the other. Forty-four of §A.17's 45 keys have exactly this shape — each is an §A.27 row as well and none carries a Remark of its own — and the forty-fifth, U+2194, is A.17/left-right-arrow/frame-unstated, where a third listing makes the same silence worse.

permitted.source: kumihan's published reading of §3.9.2's silence (docs/decisions/ambiguous-context.md): the lowest-numbered surviving class
The other survivor of §A.17 and §A.27, preferring the Western design over the Japanese one

cases.quote: For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: Three of §A.17's rows print a fullwidth compatibility glyph in the Character (字形) column against an ASCII code point in the normative UCS column: ＝ against 003D, ＜ against 003C and ＞ against 003E. §A.27 lists the same three UCS values and prints the halfwidth =, < and >, so the appendix shows both spellings of one key and states neither as the key. The quoted preamble Note is the convention that produces this, and it uses the parenthesis pair as its example. UnicodeData.txt gives U+FF1D the decomposition '<wide> 003D', so the Wide and Narrow folding ADR 0008 admits, and only that folding, carries this occurrence onto §A.17's first row; full compatibility folding is not admitted, because it would fold U+2160, a genuine cl-19 member, onto 'I'. This is not a hypothetical spelling. §3.9.2's own illustration of cl-17 reads ＝≠＜＞≦≧⊆⊇∪∩ followed by 'etc.' / 「など」, and its ten characters measure FF1D 2260 FF1C FF1E 2266 2267 2286 2287 222A 2229: three of the ten are code points §A.17 does not list and that appear nowhere in Appendix A at all. An implementation fed the document's own example text without the folding finds seven members and three unlisted characters. The code point the caller wrote asserts the full-width frame by itself and the item declares the same one, so nothing here is in tension.

permitted.source: JLReq §A preamble Note, applied to §A.17's first row (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Folding the compatibility character and then taking §A.27's row for 003D. That row is qualified 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」, and a fullwidth equals sign is the opposite declaration: U+FF1D's decomposition mapping is '<wide> 003D', so the code point the caller wrote states the frame without the item having to.

cases.quote: EN: From mathematical view point, "∪∩∧∨⊕⊗" are included in math operators (cl-18), however, in this document, these symbols are included in math symbols (cl-17) because these symbols are traditionally considered to behave in the same way as other Math symbols. — JA: “∪∩∧∨⊕⊗”は，これまでの組版上の慣習的処理から等号類に含めている．
cases.rationale: Six of §A.17's 45 members are placed here by typographic convention rather than by mathematical taxonomy, and the quoted Note is the only place the document says so. All six are in the table — 222A, 2229, 2227, 2228, 2295 and 2297 — so the table and the Note agree, but the Note is where a mathematically-motivated implementation is warned off. U+2227 LOGICAL AND is the sharpest of the six for two reasons. It is a connective rather than a relation, so nothing about it suggests 等号類 to a reader who took cl-17's Japanese name literally; and §3.9.2's own illustration of the class, ＝≠＜＞≦≧⊆⊇∪∩ followed by 'etc.' / 「など」, prints ∪ and ∩ and does not print ∧, ∨, ⊕ or ⊗. What enumerates the class is §A.17, so ∧ is a member on exactly the same footing as ＝, and this is the case an implementation that built cl-17 from the readable prose fails: with §A.17 unread, the only table reachable for 2227 is §A.27's. The Japanese Common name (通用名称) column reads 及び（合接） — 'and', the conjunction of logic — and the Appendix A preamble Note says in Japanese that the column is JIS X 0213's informative common name, so it names a reading rather than a class and changes no answer. The English half of that preamble Note omits the sentence. The two halves of the quoted Note also do not state the same thing: the English asserts that the six are mathematically cl-18 and gives a behavioral reason, and the Japanese states only the positive placement in 等号類. The exclusion from cl-18 is written down in one locale only, and that divergence is not in spec/derived/defects.tsv.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.17, nineteenth row, with §3.9.2's second Note under the cl-17 item

forbidden.why: The reading the quoted Note states and then withdraws in the same sentence. From a mathematical point of view ∧ is an operator; this document's cl-18 has six members — 002B, 2212, 00D7, 00F7, 00B1, 2213 — and 2227 is not one of them, and §A.17 lists it. An implementation that classified by mathematical category rather than by the table answers cl-18 for all six of ∪∩∧∨⊕⊗ and gets their spacing and their break behavior wrong in both of §3.7.4's settings at once, since §3.7.4 item 3 inverts the two classes' spacings against cl-24 and cl-27.
§A.27's row for 2227 is qualified 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」, which this occurrence does not declare.

cases.rationale: The far end of §A.17, stated where a reader looking for the boundary of the enumeration would look for it. U+2297 CIRCLED TIMES is the forty-fifth and last row, its Remarks cell is empty like the other forty-four, and it is also one of the six members §3.9.2's second Note places here by typographic convention. Both facts point the same way and both are worth pinning at once: an implementation that truncated the table loses its last row, and an implementation that classified by mathematical category loses the same row for the other reason, because ⊗ is a binary operation on tensors and its Japanese Common name (通用名称) says exactly that — テンソル積, tensor product. Neither ⊗ nor its neighbor ⊕ appears in §3.9.2's illustration of the class, which stops at ∪∩ and says 'etc.' / 「など」. The name is also a trap of the kind §A.18's second row sets: CIRCLED TIMES is a multiplication sign in a circle, and U+00D7 MULTIPLICATION SIGN is a cl-18 key, but a name is not a class assignment and the two keys are listed by two different tables.

forbidden.why: Reading the UCS name. CIRCLED TIMES contains the word the cl-18 key 00D7 is named for, and §3.9.2's second Note says in its English half that ⊗ is a math operator from a mathematical point of view — and then places it in cl-17. §A.18 enumerates six keys and 2297 is not among them.
§A.27's row for 2297 is qualified 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」 and this occurrence declares one em.

cases.quote: JIS X 4051 also provides similar  character classes but that are slightly different from this document. Furthermore JIS X 4051 states that it is implementation-defined how to handle characters that are not explicitly mentioned, e.g. whether they should belong to either class or not.
cases.rationale: U+2194 LEFT RIGHT ARROW is the one key of §A.17's 45 that three Appendix A tables name: §A.17 with an empty Remarks (備考) cell, §A.19 with an empty Remarks cell, and §A.27 with 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」. The §A.17 and §A.19 rows are identical character for character, down to the same Common name 同等, so nothing in the document separates the cl-17 reading from the cl-19 reading; A.19/left-right-arrow/named-by-two-classes-and-neither-qualified records that pair on the full em frame, and A.19/left-right-arrow/the-frame-decides-the-third-listing records the proportional frame, where §A.27's is the one qualified listing and the ambiguity ends. This case is the third position, where the caller declares no frame and all three listings survive. Recording it here matters because of what it shows about the tie-break rather than about the arrow: classification.ambiguous_context offers exactly two choices, the lowest-numbered survivor and the highest-numbered one, and over the survivor set {cl-17, cl-19, cl-27} they reach cl-17 and cl-27 and no choice of that question reaches cl-19. The middle survivor is equally permitted by the document and is selected by nothing in the policy space. Both reachable readings are recorded below and the unreachable one is stated here rather than dropped, because a case that recorded two of three equally permitted answers would be laundering a silence into a requirement. That the question is under-specified for a degree-three key is reported as a finding against spec/derived/questions.tsv, not repaired inside a case.

permitted.source: kumihan's published reading of §3.9.2's silence (docs/decisions/ambiguous-context.md): the lowest-numbered surviving class, which is §A.17's
The highest-numbered survivor of §A.17, §A.19 and §A.27, preferring the Western design over the Japanese one

cases.quote: ＜ 003C LESS-THAN SIGN 不等号（より小）
cases.rationale: Twenty-five Appendix A entries key on an ordered pair of code points — §A.27 lists <02E5, 02E9> and <02E9, 02E5> as two distinct members, and §A.11, §A.15 and §A.16 key the combining semi-voiced kana the same way — so an Appendix A key is a sequence and a longest-match scan over the tables is the only correct lookup. cl-17 contributes no such entry: each of §A.17's 45 rows holds a single UCS value, and the class holds no code-point sequence at all. This case asserts that, and it asserts it at the one place in this class where a plausible implementation would invent one. `<=` is how every programming language and every plain-text document spells 'less than or equal', and §A.17 lists 2266 LESS-THAN OVER EQUAL TO ≦ as a single key, so an implementation reconciling the two by adding a two-code-point key rooted at U+003C matches across these two items and must then refuse the stream, since the key would begin in one occurrence and end in the next. The second occurrence is the one asked about, because that is the ordinal a spurious pair key would swallow. The far end of the same reasoning is A.17/less-than-or-equal-to/unlisted-code-point: U+2264 ≤, the single code point the digraph usually denotes, is in no Appendix A table.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.17, first row, matched as a single-code-point key in the occurrence following §A.17's ninth row (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.27's row for 003D is qualified 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」 and this occurrence declares one em. The neighboring ＜ decides nothing either: no Appendix A key begins at U+003C and continues.

cases.quote: There are some punctuation marks that are used uniquely in either vertical writing mode or horizontal writing mode.
cases.rationale: cl-17 has no direction-conditional membership, and this case is where that is written down. §3.1.1 is where the document restricts a member to one writing mode, and Appendix A carries those restrictions in the Remarks (備考) column: exactly twelve keys carry one, spread over §A.1, §A.2, §A.5, §A.6, §A.7 and §A.8, and each reads 'used in vertical composition' / 「縦組で使用」 or 'used in horizontal composition' / 「横組で使用」. None of §A.17's 45 keys is among them: its Remarks column is empty in every row and in both renderings, and the other two tables naming these keys say only 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」 (§A.27) and nothing (§A.19, for 2194 alone). U+21D2 RIGHTWARDS DOUBLE ARROW is the member where the temptation is strongest, because an arrow names a direction in its own UCS name and vertical writing rotates the line it sits on; the class does not move. The case names the direction on purpose, which is unusual here: the direction-parity gate composes a case that names none in both modes and requires identical results, so the invariance is already proved over every other case in this file, and this one states it where a reader looking for cl-17's direction behavior would look for it. §3.7.4's Note on independent-line placement does describe a vertical convention — the Japanese half rotates the formula 90 degrees clockwise and indents it from the line head — but it says 例が多い, 'in most cases', and it is a placement of the formula rather than a membership of the class.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.17, thirty-eighth row; no Remarks cell of §A.17 names a writing mode (§3.1.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.27's row for 21D2 is qualified 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」 and this occurrence declares one em, in vertical writing as in horizontal. A writing mode is not a frame (字幅), and no Remark anywhere in Appendix A makes any cl-17 key conditional on one.

cases.quote: Breaking a line is allowed before or after the following character classes even though Table 2 prohibits it.
cases.rationale: §C.3 lists four levels of kinsoku (禁則, line-break prohibition) convention, and cl-17 is named in none of them. It is named nowhere in Appendix B, C, D or E at all: the string 'cl-17' occurs in the rendering only in the table of contents, in §3.7.4, in §3.9.2 and in §A.17's own heading, so the whole of what the document says about a math symbol (等号類) beyond its 45 keys is in those two sections, and Table 1 and Table 2 are published only as the PDFs spec/PROVENANCE.toml records as absent by design. The contrast is inside §3.9.2 itself, which for three subjects does state a reclassification — 々 is regarded as cl-19, ー as cl-16, and the small kana as cl-15 or cl-16, each conditioned on relaxing the line-head prohibition — and states nothing of the kind for cl-17, whose two Notes are about the origin of the class and about the six convention members. So the class of this occurrence is invariant across the whole relaxation surface, and the three entries below form a chain over the two questions that describe that surface rather than asserting the invariance once. This matters more for cl-17 than for most classes, because §3.7.4 item 4 does state a break permission and a break priority for it — a line may be broken between cl-17 and an adjacent cl-24, cl-27 or cl-21, and in an independent formula line cl-17 is the first place to try — and neither is a change of class. An implementation that discharged a break preference by moving an equals sign into some other class would change its spacing and its matrix answers everywhere, not only at the break the level was about.

permitted.source: JLReq alternative (§C.3 level 1, the loosest of the four, which names cl-03, cl-04, cl-05, cl-08, cl-09, cl-10, cl-11, cl-12 and cl-13 and not cl-17)
JLReq alternative (§C.3 with §C.2 notes 1 to 3 read as a change of class rather than as an override of Table 2)

cases.quote: EN: Because the math symbols, such as SQUARE ROOT "√", INTEGRAL "∫" and GREEK CAPITAL LETTER SIGMA "Σ", are not frequently used in common books, the handling of these math symbols is considered to be out of scope for this document. Also, mathematical and scientific notations like numerical formulae are out of scope for this document. — JA: 理工学書などでは，水平の罫線を使用した分数（やぐら組ともよばれている），根号式，積分記号，総和記号なども使用される．これらの記号は，一般書ではそれほど使用されていないので，この文書では，これらの処理は範囲としない．
cases.rationale: The boundary of cl-17 that §3.7.4 draws in a sentence, and the one an implementation is most likely to cross. √ is a mathematical symbol set full-width in Japanese books, it sits inside the formulae §3.7.4 is about, and the section that defines cl-17 names it — to exclude it. Appendix A agrees and says where it goes instead: U+221A is listed by §A.19 with an empty Remarks cell and by §A.27 with 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」, and by no other table, so on the declared full em frame the one surviving listing is §A.19's and the answer is cl-19. U+222B INTEGRAL and U+03A3 GREEK CAPITAL LETTER SIGMA are listed by exactly the same two tables and answer the same way. The exclusion is one of the places the two locales do not state the same rule, so both halves are quoted. The English names √, ∫ and Σ and adds a sentence excluding formula notation generally; the Japanese instead names built-up fractions (やぐら組), radicals, integral signs and summation signs — the built-up fraction is in neither the English list nor anywhere else in the English half — and carries no sentence about formula notation. The scope of §3.7.4, which is the only section stating cl-17's frame and its spacings, therefore differs by locale, and that divergence is not in spec/derived/defects.tsv. Note also what the English half names: GREEK CAPITAL LETTER SIGMA is U+03A3, a letter, and not U+2211 N-ARY SUMMATION, which no Appendix A table lists at all.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.19's listing of 221A, against §A.27's Remarks column (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Extending the class by mathematical kinship. √ is a math symbol in the ordinary sense and is set one em wide in Japanese books, which is exactly §3.7.4 item 1's statement about cl-17, and the two facts together make this the most natural wrong answer for the class. §A.17 enumerates 45 keys and 221A is not one of them, and §3.7.4's own Note declares the handling of √ out of scope. A class whose membership grew by resemblance would also swallow ∫ and Σ, both of which §A.19 and §A.27 list and §A.17 does not.
§A.27's row for 221A is qualified 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」, which an occurrence declared one em wide does not satisfy.

cases.quote: EN: In JIS X 4051, math symbols (＋－÷×etc.) and math operators (＝≠＜＞≦≧⊆⊇∪∩etc.) are included in the "Japanese characters excluded from 1. to 12." class or Western character class. However, handling of math symbols and math operators adjacent to Western character or Arabic numerals is different from kanji. So, in this document, new math operators (cl-18) and math symbols (cl-17) classes are defined. — JA: 数式などに使う演算記号（＋－÷×等）や等号類（＝≠＜＞≦≧⊆⊇∪∩等）は，JIS X 4051では漢字などと同じ文字クラス（1.～12.以外の和字）又は欧文用文字に含まれている．しかし，欧字やアラビア数字と連続した場合の扱いは，漢字とは異なるので，次項の演算記号とともに新たな文字クラスを作成した．
cases.rationale: The boundary of cl-17 stated from the other side, and the document's own sentence is what pushes an implementation across it. The quoted Note hangs off §3.9.2's cl-17 item — the cl-18 item carries no Note of its own — and its two halves do not state the same thing. The English calls ＋－÷× 'math symbols', which is cl-17's English name, and ＝≠＜＞≦≧⊆⊇∪∩ 'math operators', which is cl-18's; the Japanese calls the first group 演算記号 and the second 等号類, agreeing with the two list items the Note sits under, with §3.9.2's illustrations, and with §A.17 and §A.18. The English half therefore calls cl-17's own members cl-18's and cl-18's members cl-17's, and it contradicts itself inside one paragraph, since it closes by saying that new math operators (cl-18) and math symbols (cl-17) classes are defined. A reader working from the English alone gets the two classes exactly backwards, and every one of the 51 keys involved is then wrong at once. U+00D7 MULTIPLICATION SIGN is the test: it is one of the four glyphs the swapped English sentence calls a math symbol, and §A.17's 45 rows do not list it while §A.18's third row does. This project reads the Japanese, which is also what the tables state. The divergence is the same shape as the one already recorded as b2-note-7-locale-class-divergence and it is absent from spec/derived/defects.tsv; that absence is reported as a finding rather than repaired by a case.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.18, third row, and §3.9.2's cl-18 illustration; the Japanese half of the cl-17 item's first Note (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Reading the English half of §3.9.2's first Note under the cl-17 item as a class assignment. It calls ＋－÷× math symbols, which is the English name of cl-17, while §A.17's 45 rows do not list 00D7 and §A.18's six do. An implementation built from that sentence rather than from the tables puts all six cl-18 members into cl-17 and all 45 cl-17 members into cl-18, and since §3.7.4 item 3 gives the two classes opposite spacings against cl-24 and cl-27 in an independent formula line, and item 4's Note orders cl-17 ahead of cl-18 as a break position, the error is visible in the composed line and not only in a class number.
§A.27's row for 00D7 is qualified 'proportionally-spaced' / 「プロポーショナル」, which this occurrence does not declare.

cases.quote: JIS X 4051 also provides similar  character classes but that are slightly different from this document. Furthermore JIS X 4051 states that it is implementation-defined how to handle characters that are not explicitly mentioned, e.g. whether they should belong to either class or not.
cases.rationale: §A.17 lists U+2266 LESS-THAN OVER EQUAL TO ≦ and U+2267 GREATER-THAN OVER EQUAL TO ≧ as its eleventh and twelfth rows. It does not list U+2264 LESS-THAN OR EQUAL TO ≤ or U+2265 GREATER-THAN OR EQUAL TO ≥, and no Appendix A table lists either of them anywhere. That is the more consequential half of the boundary than any exclusion the document argues for, because ≤ is what most keyboards, most editors and most mathematical software produce for the relation ≦ denotes, and the two glyphs differ only in whether the lower stroke is parallel or slanted. The absence is not a judgment about the relation: §A's preamble bounds every one of its tables to the non-ideographic characters of ISO/IEC 10646 collection 285 'BASIC JAPANESE' and collection 286 'JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHICS EXTENSION', so a gap in the enumeration is a repertoire boundary rather than an exclusion, and the quoted sentence is what the document says instead — that the question is implementation-defined. An answer here is therefore a published reading and never a requirement, which is why the standing is unstated and both readings appear. On the ideographic frame the two agree, and recording the agreement is what makes the disagreement legible: A.19/up-down-arrow/unlisted-on-the-proportional-frame is where they part, and neither reading reaches cl-17 on any frame, because extending an enumeration to a code point that looks like one of its members is not one of the two choices. This is the far end of A.17/less-than-and-equals-sign/no-code-point-sequence: an implementation that invented a `<=` sequence key would be inventing precisely the member JLReq declines to enumerate.

permitted.source: The unconditional reading: every unlisted occurrence is cl-19

forbidden.why: Adding an unlisted relation to the class its lookalikes are in. §A.17 lists 2266 and 2267 and does not list 2264 or 2265, and §3.9.2 records that the handling of a character the lists do not mention is implementation-defined — not that the answer is the nearest table. A reading that extended an enumeration by glyph resemblance would have to decide the same question for U+2A7D, U+2A7E and every other relation Unicode encodes, and the document draws no line for it to follow.
